name: Babadjou (Mbasso)
overview: The majority people of the Bamboutos, the Babadjou (Mbasso) speak ngomba'e, a language specific to the grouping. Mostly coming from Bapa (North-West), they are organised around the paramount chief, the colleges of the 9 and of the 7 notables and ritual servants; coffee, livestock and subsistence crops sustain them, and the Lehere festival closes each year.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: The grouping describes itself as unique of its kind in Cameroon; it is the majority in the Bamboutos.
Some also speak the language of Bapa (North-West); Baligam from the North-West live among them.
The Babadjou most often marry outside the group, men and women alike.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land that belongs to them.
The majority came from Bapa, in the North-West, and found a few inhabitants there; ties with the North-West remain very close.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: The paramount chief relies on two colleges of notables, the 9 (pekem lepfo) and the 7 (pekem sambu), on his servants (tchuo'nto') and his great servants (tchinda).
The notables deliberate, the chief approves and his servants announce the decision to the population, which carries it out.
Each caste has its envoy and anyone can speak freely; everyone knows their place, in harmony.

Permanent societies: the supreme magni (mothers of twins renowned by the chief), who guide new mothers of twins; the tchuo'nto', who accompany the sick chief, bury him, announce his death and purify the village after a violent death.
In the past, in mourning, the woman sat on the ground, gave up her place to the man, and bowed to greet him.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: The woman leaves her family for that of her husband.
Majority at 21 for a boy; a girl becomes a woman at puberty. Stated ages: 21 for men, 18 for women.
Steps: meeting of the families, engagement, marriage proposal, bride price.

Bride price: billy goat, goat, can of oil, money, white wine and drinks. Ritual elements: raffia wine (appeasement and happiness), the ox horn, the nshui-ndzap herb, mahogany (epeu) and red oil, bearers of blessing.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Cult of the wangea tree to renew oneself, cult of sacred places, consulting the ancestors in case of serious trouble.

Sacred places: the Ndumvu waterfall; Mangwa, on Mount Bamboutos, where the white earth (mbouo ngong) used in the rites comes from; Magni-Monghe, a small stone basin with an inexhaustible liquid used by diviners; Tchou, still water used to call the rain in times of drought; Nda'nkong (Toumaka), where two twins parted; La'ndem (Bamedouso), where people went to fetch bees to drive out the Germans.
Birth may be the return of a forebear; some deaths are a return to origins, others divine punishments. The dead remain close and reveal the future.
Forbidden day (mbi' ih): no one farms, buries or travels. The sacred wangheu tree planted in the courtyard is not burned; a pregnant woman does not cut banana leaves and does not go to the river.
Taboos: murder, adultery, theft; the murderer was banished and any offence against the chief's wife severely punished.
The chief's messages are transmitted at night by the tchinda.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: coffee, gardening, livestock rearing. Women: farming, livestock rearing.
The land goes to the first occupants; it is obtained by gift, inheritance or purchase.
Ancestral crafts: masks, drums, carved stools, mortars, baskets.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Traditional ndap attire, raffia fibres, frayed sacks for dances; wrappers for women.
Traditional practitioners and diviners are widely consulted, notably for childbirth.
Beauty: traditional dress, strength and musculature for men; adornment, full figure and hard work for women.
Courtship: the man hard-working, responsible, protective and complimentary; the woman hard-working, gentle and a good cook.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Dances: ndzang (balafon, drum, castanets) at funerals and at the chief's coming out; ntsebeu at the coming out of the chief of the la'akam; lehere (flute, drum) at the festival; makongue at births, funerals, twin ceremonies and bride price ceremonies; mbaya at mourning, births and bride price ceremonies; samali for meetings.
Festival: the Lehere festival, from 24 to 31 December.

sections.title: The names
items: Fo and Nʉzeu are names for twins.
The name honours the circumstances of the birth, a chief or a dear person; it may change once (inheritance, new status, initiation).
A person is honoured by placing taa, ndzeu or nde before their name: Tafo, Kafo, Tchofo, Ndefombasso, Ndzeugang.
The founder, Tchui-tsəm teuh (“piece of tree”), is the one who sets the example.

lessons.title: Who are the Babadjou (Mbasso)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Babadjou (Mbasso) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Babadjou (Mbasso) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Babadjou (Mbasso) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Babadjou (Mbasso) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Babadjou (Mbasso) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Babadjou (Mbasso) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The grouping describes itself as unique of its kind in Cameroon; it is the majority in the Bamboutos. • Some also speak the language of Bapa (North-West); Baligam from the North-West live among them. • The Babadjou most often marry outside the group, men and women alike. • Ancestral land that belongs to them. • The majority came from Bapa, in the North-West, and found a few inhabitants there; ties with the North-West remain very close.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The majority people of the Bamboutos, the Babadjou (Mbasso) speak ngomba'e, a language specific to the grouping. Mostly coming from Bapa (North-West), they are organised around the paramount chief, the colleges of the 9 and of the 7 notables and ritual servants; coffee, livestock and subsistence crops sustain them, and the Lehere festival closes each year.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Babadjou (Mbasso) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Babadjou (Mbasso)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment

vocabulary.langText: couscous de maïs, sauce gombo et légumes

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Babadjou (Mbasso), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Babadjou (Mbasso).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Babadjou (Mbasso), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Babadjou (Mbasso).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: taro in yellow sauce, kontchaf (maize and beans), maize couscous, okra sauce and greens. • Drinks: raffia wine, palm wine, maize wine. • Men: coffee, gardening, livestock rearing. Women: farming, livestock rearing.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Babadjou (Mbasso) mainly eat taro in yellow sauce, kontchaf, maize couscous, okra sauce and vegetables. Traditional drinks: raffia wine, palm wine, maize wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Babadjou (Mbasso): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Babadjou (Mbasso), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Babadjou (Mbasso) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Dances: ndzang (balafon, drum, castanets) at funerals and when the chief comes out; ntsebeu when the chief of the la'akam comes out; lehere (flute, drum) at the festival; makongue at births, funerals, twin ceremonies and bride price ceremonies; mbaya at mourning, births and bride price ceremonies; samali for gatherings. • Festival: the Lehere festival, from 24 to 31 December.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Babadjou (Mbasso), traditional dances (funerals, lehere, makongue) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: balafon, drum, castanets, flute. Festival(s): 24-31 December.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Babadjou (Mbasso) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I understand
activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Babadjou (Mbasso), traditional dances (funerals, lehere, makongue) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: balafon, drum, castanets, flute. Festival(s): 24-31 December.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Babadjou (Mbasso)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Babadjou (Mbasso), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Babadjou (Mbasso). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Babadjou (Mbasso), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Babadjou (Mbasso). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: coffee, gardening, livestock. Women: farming, livestock. • Land goes to the first occupants; it is obtained by gift, inheritance or purchase. • Ancestral crafts: masks, drums, carved stools, mortars, baskets.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: coffee, gardening, livestock rearing. Women: farming, livestock rearing. Land goes to the first occupants; it is obtained by gift, inheritance or purchase.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Babadjou (Mbasso)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Babadjou (Mbasso)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Babadjou (Mbasso), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Babadjou (Mbasso). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Babadjou (Mbasso), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Babadjou (Mbasso). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Worship of the wangea tree to renew oneself, worship of sacred places, consulting the ancestors in case of serious trouble. • Sacred places: the Ndumvu waterfall; Mangwa, on Mount Bamboutos, source of the white earth (mbouo ngong) used in rites; Magni-Monghe, a small stone basin with an inexhaustible liquid used by diviners; Tchou, still water used to call the rain in times of drought; Nda'nkong (Toumaka), where two twins parted; La'ndem (Bamedouso), where people went to fetch bees to drive out the Germans. • A birth may be the return of an ancestor; some deaths are a return to the origins, others divine punishments. The dead remain close and reveal the future. • Forbidden day (mbi' ih): no one farms, buries or travels. The sacred wangheu tree planted in the courtyard is not burnt; a pregnant woman does not cut banana leaves and does not go to the river. • Taboos: murder, adultery, theft; the murderer was banished and an offence against the chief's wife was severely punished.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cult of the wangea tree to renew oneself, cult of sacred places, consulting the ancestors in case of serious trouble. Sacred places: the Ndumvu waterfall; Mangwa, on Mount Bamboutos, where the white earth (mbouo ngong) used in rites comes from; Magni-Monghe, a small stone basin with an unfailing liquid used by diviners; Tchou, still water for calling the rain in case of drought; Nda'nkong (Toumaka), where two twins parted; La'ndem (Bamedouso), where people went to fetch bees to drive out the Germans.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Babadjou (Mbasso) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Ngomba'e
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Babadjou (Mbasso) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Babadjou (Mbasso) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Babadjou (Mbasso) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Babadjou (Mbasso) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Ngomba'e. • Greetings: Ntsyje’te ? = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); O zamɛ́ɛ̄ ? = morning greeting (one person); Pe zhamɛ́ɛ̄ ? = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Ta:’ / mo’ó, púó, Tā:r, Kuə, Ta:. • The founder, Tchui-tsəm teuh (“piece of tree”), is the one who sets the example.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Ngomba'e are the first steps towards communicating with the Babadjou (Mbasso). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Ngomba'e.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Ngomba'e are the first steps towards communicating with the Babadjou (Mbasso). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
